doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Where his sound came from: his father and the age of distinct sounds
summary: He credits his father for his sound concept and contrasts past players with distinct sounds with today's mediocrity, with stories of Billy Higgins and Papa Jo Jones.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: That’s a great statement and I wonder if the way you sound and play comes out of that. Because when I listen to you I hear a lot more stepping out than I do from some people, with your glissandos I guess I’d call it. And sometimes not constant walk but loping from one thing to the next. It’s hard to describe. But you have a sound that no one else has. And I was going to ask, I might as well ask you now, do you know where your concept of a sound came from?

My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after.
